advisories.text: Read the two strips at the top. The first is the hour, the power in the pool, and how much infection is in your kit. The second is the four things worth doing aboard, all four tracked, with a mark against the one you said you came up here for. Finish any of them and the run is a win.

You do not have to stay on the route you declared. If the shuttle stops being reachable, the bridge, comms and the hold are all still open — and the trackers tell you where each of them stands without you having to work it out.

The line under the schematic is what the things you can see will do if you end the hour now. If it says something reaches you, it will, and it will cost you a capability. Move, seal, brace, or throw something loud somewhere else — all four are cheaper than the wound.

You only see what is in this compartment or next door. A hollow mark in lower case is where you last saw something, not where it is. LISTEN reaches three compartments and tells you what each contact is doing.

Walking is heard three compartments away. Creeping is heard one. That is the whole difference and it is the most important number in the game: a sound tells everything in range that you are HERE, and here is where they go.
Nothing aboard knows where you are. It knows where the last noise was. Get out of the compartment quietly and it arrives, finds nothing, searches for an hour and gives up on you.
The marks at the end of the top line are what is left of this hour. One thing from your hand each hour is free to play or to set aside; everything after that costs time.

Your hand stays with you between hours — nothing is thrown away at the end of one. Setting something aside costs nothing once an hour and draws you a replacement, so a hand you cannot use is a hand you can clear out.

There is a weapon in your kit now. It rolls against whatever you point it at, and a miss empties it until the armory refills it. Combat is expensive and losing them is cheap: running is usually right.
This compartment is one point from drawing something new out of the dark. Noise fades by one an hour, so an hour spent quietly here fixes it.
Something is loose. There is a hard cap on how many of them the ship will hold at once — when it is full, the pressure goes into the hold instead, and what is in the hold is worse than another STRAY.

The bar marked THE HOLD is how close the MOTHER is to standing up. Every hour fills it a little; noise in the ore hold fills it faster. When it is full she comes, she does not lose you, and nothing you are carrying can kill her. What you can do is cost her time.

That is the MOTHER. Do not swing at it. A bulkhead in its face holds it an hour, flooding the vents from the bridge holds it two, and anything loud thrown into another compartment sends it the wrong way. Every one of those buys you hours you still need.

A wound takes two things: something you could do, gone for the rest of the run, and one more infection into your own kit. The infection is not hidden — the count is on the top strip. When there is nothing left you can do, neither are you.

Infection in your hand costs you while you hold it, and it cannot be given up to a wound. Setting it aside stops it for the hour; only the MEDBAY takes it out of your kit for good, and that costs time and power but never a wound.
You are one short of the CARRIER line. Launching at or above it still gets you off the ship, at a worse weighting. Two hours in the medbay, or a different route entirely, are both still open.

Every compartment holds two things and searching is heard two compartments away. Almost all the power in this run is in the ship rather than in the reactor: if you are not searching, you are not funding anything.
That weapon is empty until the ARMORY refills it, for one time and one power. Something in your hand that cannot fire is something you can set aside.
The pool is nearly full and power over the cap is power thrown away. Spend it: into the shuttle, into a bulkhead, or into the medbay.
Bank it. Power in the pool does nothing for the shuttle until it is in the shuttle, and the pool is not safe.
The reactor is not at full output. Each repair is two time for one more power an hour, and it pays back every hour after that — the relay in particular cannot be held without it.
Nothing walks in the crawlspace. A CRAWLER does not walk, so it is the one thing that can follow you in. Coming out of a hatch is loud enough to draw, and you cannot swing properly on the way out.

The shuttle is out of reach on the hours left. That is not the run over: the overload on the bridge, the relay at comms and the specimen in the hold all end the run as a win, and the trackers say how far each one has to go.
The shuttle has what it needs. Everything you do from here is a bet against the infection count and the hours left.
Three things left you can still do. The next wound takes one of them. Finish something or get somewhere nothing can reach you.
